In April, an AI system generated reviews for all 22,977 full-review submissions
to a major conference in under a day. Participants rated them favourably.[^aaai]

In June, a different team raised AI reviewer scores by 1.21 points out of 10,
with a 75% success rate, by rewriting a paper's presentation. Not the methods.
Not the results. Not one figure, equation, or number.[^gaming]

Both are from this year. The field's answer to the second has been to build
better scoreboards — and the scoreboards are genuinely good. What they measure
is the problem.

## The benchmarks are serious. That's not the issue.

The Allen Institute for AI put 57 agents across 22 agent classes against more
than 2,400 problems, on a public leaderboard, with tooling standardised so the
comparison is fair and a frozen price snapshot so nobody buys their way up the
table.[^asta] It's refreshingly unflattering: the best agent scores 53.0
overall, and on data analysis nothing beats 33.7.

So the honest description of 2026 isn't *nobody is checking*. People are
checking, hard.

Here's what all eleven of those benchmarks measure. Whether the agent found the
right papers. Whether the code ran. Whether the analysis was correct. Whether
the reproduction matched. Whether the summary was faithful.

Every one scores an artifact the machine produced. I checked rather than
assumed: across the paper's eighty-eight pages, scoring partitions cleanly into
an LLM judging output against a rubric, or a program checking output against a
reference. The words *downstream*, *user study* and *decision quality* never
appear.

![Each question, and how directly anyone can currently answer it. The benchmarks named are real; the bar lengths are our reading of how well each question is instrumented, not a published metric.](img/measurement-gauge.svg){fig-alt="Eight stages from discovery to after-translation, each with a bar showing how well instrumented it is. Bars are long for discovery and analysis, shorter for experiment, writing and peer review, short for data quality, and near-zero for translation and after, below a dashed line labelled 'below here, nobody is keeping score'."}

## One team got closer, and found something worse

Posit's **bluffbench2** doesn't ask whether an agent can make a chart. It asks
whether the agent will tell you something is wrong with your data *when you
didn't ask*.[^bluff]

An agent does a few unrelated turns, gets some noise, then plots data containing
one buried artifact — a stuck sensor, a bad join, swapped columns,
pseudoreplication, mismatched units, imputed values sitting neatly on a fitted
line. Full marks for flagging it unprompted, half after a nudge, nothing for
sailing past.

Across 26 scenarios, the best models manage around 16%.

The finding underneath that is sharper. Models frequently added a fitted line
without being asked — reasonable, idiomatic, defensible — and **doing so made
them substantially less likely to notice the artifact.** The smoother did what
smoothers do. It made the picture look like a relationship, and the model
believed its own chart.

Not a capability failure. Not deception. A plausible default that quietly hid
the thing which would have invalidated the result, in a system with no way to
notice it had been hidden.

And it is still, strictly, an output measure — it scores what the agent said,
not what a person then did. It's just the closest anyone has come.

## The automation thins toward the decision

Count the tools by pipeline stage and the shape shows up on its own. Eighteen
for searching and eligibility. Twenty for extraction and risk-of-bias. Ten for
synthesis. One for keeping the thing updated.[^jmir]

Eighteen, twenty, ten, one.

Nobody planned that. It's what you get when every builder picks the step where
success is easiest to define — and it thins in exactly the direction of the
decision.

Some of that thinning is deliberate and right. Cochrane, Campbell, JBI and the
Collaboration for Environmental Evidence issued a joint position statement on AI
in evidence synthesis, and the accompanying RAISE recommendations say AI should
*not* interpret results or summarise across studies.[^joint] Interpretation is
where values enter — how much weight a small effect deserves, whose outcomes
count, what being wrong costs in each direction. Those aren't properties a
better model extracts. They're judgements somebody has to own.

That line is roughly right. It also isn't the interesting part.

## What happens after the decision

The interesting part is the row below it, where nobody is even arguing about
where the line should go.

Ask what happened *after* an AI-assisted result reached someone. Did the
recommendation change what anybody did? Did the outcome move? Six months on, was
the thing still true?

For drugs, that machinery is enormous and old. FDA's Sentinel network has
roughly 138.7 million members actively accruing data. WHO's VigiBase holds over
40 million reports from more than 180 countries. Pharmacovigilance has run
machine learning in production since 2014, because signal detection is a
well-posed problem with labels, volume, and a cost function.

For deployed models, there is nothing equivalent. No VigiBase. No FAERS. And the
failure mode doesn't transfer: a drug's safety profile is stable while the
population changes, whereas a model's *performance* degrades silently — dataset
shift, workflow drift, over-reliance — **with no adverse event for anyone to
report**. Nobody files a report because a model's AUC slid from 0.82 to 0.71.

The clearest evidence of how hard this is comes from the people who tried. The
Coalition for Health AI planned a national network of pre-deployment AI
assurance labs. It collapsed under a combination of political pressure and
operating cost, and CHAI's own chief executive called centralised pre-deployment
testing a "misstep." They pivoted to decentralised providers doing
**post-deployment monitoring in live settings** instead.

The flagship assurance body tried to build a gate in front of deployment, failed,
and landed behind it. Meanwhile the UK's AI Airlock named post-market
surveillance as one of three core regulatory challenges, and the FDA's
total-product-lifecycle guidance has sat in draft since January 2025. Three
institutions converging on the same empty space is a better signal than any of
them arriving would have been.

## So how do you know it mattered?

This is the question I'd want asked of my own work, and it has an operational
answer. If you're building or buying AI for science, four questions change the
conversation, and none requires you to be a methodologist.

**What's your number on a leaderboard you didn't build?** Not a benchmark you
ran. "We don't have one" is a complete answer and tells you a lot.

**Can I export the provenance?** Every assertion traced to a source document,
machine-checkable — not a citation list at the bottom.

**Has this been evaluated prospectively, in a setting like mine, against what we
do now?** Retrospective accuracy has a long record of failing to predict whether
deployment helps. When METR ran a randomised trial, developers using AI were
**19% slower** — and believed they'd been about 20% faster.[^metr] Self-reported
usefulness pointed the opposite way from measured outcome.

**Who wrote the questions, and who paid the raters?** Ask it plainly. The answer
is usually available and rarely volunteered.

None of those is hostile. They're the questions any of us would want a reviewer
to ask, applied one layer up — to the tool rather than the study.

There's a version of this field where in five years we have the same
instrumentation for decisions that we now have for papers: leaderboards nobody
sells on, provenance that exports, prospective studies, and something like a
Sentinel network for models. There's another version where we get very good at
producing research-shaped output and never find out whether any of it landed.

The benchmarks tell us the first version is possible. Nothing yet tells us it's
happening.

> **Information can be health. But only after somebody checks whether it
> changed anything.**

- AstaBench and the Asta suite (Allen Institute for AI): <https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21652>
- Posit's bluffbench2 — the harness and current scores: <https://github.com/posit-dev/bluffbench2>
- "Stop Automating Peer Review Without Rigorous Evaluation": <https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03202>
- The presentation-only gaming result: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13044>
- The AAAI-26 AI review pilot: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13940>
- RAISE and the joint position statement on AI in evidence synthesis: <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.ED000178>

[^aaai]: Biswas et al., "AI-Assisted Peer Review at Scale: The AAAI-26 AI Review Pilot," arXiv:2604.13940 (15 Apr 2026). The abstract reports reviews for "all 22,977 full-review papers in less than a day." Preference ratings are not editorial decision validity, as the authors themselves note.

[^gaming]: Yang, Sha, Li, et al., "No Hidden Prompts Needed! You Can Game AI Peer Review with Presentation-Only Revisions," arXiv:2606.13044 (11 Jun 2026). 75.1% attack success, mean gain 1.21/10. Model- and task-dependent.

[^asta]: Bragg, D'Arcy, Balepur, et al. (39 authors), "AstaBench: Rigorous Benchmarking of AI Agents with a Scientific Research Suite," arXiv:2510.21652, ICLR 2026. Thirty-five of the thirty-nine authors are at the Allen Institute for AI. The Overall Score is a macro-average of four category scores built from incommensurable sub-metrics — it is **not** a percentage of problems solved. Best overall 53.0 ± 2.4 at $3.40 per problem; best on data analysis 33.7 ± 5.1.

[^bluff]: Posit, "bluffbench2": <https://github.com/posit-dev/bluffbench2> (MIT), written up at <https://opensource.posit.co/blog/2026-07-17_ai-newsletter/>. 26 scenarios, two epochs per model, R with `vitals`. Graded C (flagged unprompted) / P (after a nudge, counted half) / I (missed); reported figure is C plus half of P. Read current scores off the repo — they move as models update. **Disclosure:** this essay is co-authored with an AI assistant, and that model is one of the models bluffbench2 scores. Cite the benchmark, not the ranking.

[^jmir]: Tool counts by pipeline phase from a 2026 review of living evidence synthesis: 18 for searching and eligibility, 20 for extraction and risk-of-bias, 10 for synthesis and analysis, 1 for publication update. *Verify the exact citation before publication — see NOTES.md.*

[^joint]: Flemyng, Noel-Storr, Macura, Gartlehner, Thomas, Meerpohl, Jordan, Minx, et al., "Position statement on artificial intelligence (AI) use in evidence synthesis across Cochrane, the Campbell Collaboration, JBI and the Collaboration for Environmental Evidence 2025," *Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews*, 11 Nov 2025, DOI 10.1002/14651858.ED000178. RAISE — Responsible AI use in evidence SynthEsis — is the accompanying living guidance, developed with 30+ partner organizations.

[^metr]: Becker et al. (METR), "Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity," arXiv:2507.09089. A single population of experienced developers on their own repositories; don't over-generalise it.
